indicators.note: the letters are one possible rearrangement of what is printed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters; the apostrophe is ignored

explanation.surface: A remark on what kind of clothing an idler tends to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks what sort of garment a lounger wears, and the lounger's sort is exactly what gets rearranged. Long trousers are the grown-up alternative to a schoolboy's shorts.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: long trousers are one kind of garment, the full-length leg covering.

blocks.note: the River Lee flows through east London into the Thames
the possessive supplies its S

explanation.surface: A note on the mud that settles on the bed of a river in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive does double duty: in the surface it links river to sediment, and in the wordplay it simply adds its S. The Lee (or Lea) is a tributary of the Thames in east London.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though a narrow one: the word is used chiefly for the dregs that settle out of wine.

blocks.note: the surface wants a landmark or attraction; the setter means a part of the face
the surface means stunning; read literally, it means taking in breath

explanation.surface: Praise for some stunning landmark or attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: Breathtaking usually means stunning; taken literally it means drawing air in, and the facial feature that does that is the nostril.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading: the nostril is the facial feature through which air is drawn, so it takes breath.

clue.text: Tory changes new test for garments (3,2)

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase used for a verb phrase; a try-on is the test itself

blocks.note: anagram fodder
N = new, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician revises a new test, as if for school uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory looks like a political subject changing policy; it is just four letters to be mixed with the N from new.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: putting clothes on in a shop to see whether they fit is a test for garments.

indicators.note: the letters are rubbish, i.e. in a mess

blocks.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An instruction to take the rubbish out to the bin.
explanation.walkthrough: Rubbish sits in the surface as the thing being carried out, and it is the instruction to jumble the words beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the more formal word for acquiring something.

indicators.note: the letters are confused, mixed up

blocks.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A designer's template turns out to baffle the customers.
explanation.walkthrough: Confusing reads as an adjective describing the template, but it is an instruction acting on clients.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: a cut-out sheet through which paint is applied to reproduce a design is a template.

clue.text: Bird returns gold to garbage can (5)

indicators.note: goes back, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: OR is gold in heraldry; turned round it is RO
a bin is a garbage can

explanation.surface: A bird brings some gold back to a rubbish bin.
explanation.walkthrough: Returns looks like the bird flying home, but it acts on the gold. Heraldic OR for gold is one of the setter's commonest tools.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the robin is one familiar garden bird.

blocks.note: re = regarding, as in memo headers
verse = poetry

explanation.surface: A critic's comment that poetry has gone backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes Regarding poetry look like a heading for a remark about literature; it is two plain pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, most familiar from driving, where a car goes into reverse.

blocks.note: points to a form of writing: a short prose composition
reads as a vague effort, but it is also the old meaning of the answer word itself

explanation.walkthrough: The word essay comes from the French essayer, to try, so an essay is literally a literary attempt, and to essay something still means to attempt it.
explanation.definitionFit: An etymological fit: the short prose composition takes its name from the old verb meaning to try.

clue.text: Elm Bert chopped up for quiver (7)

indicators.note: cut into pieces that are put back in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An elm is felled by someone named Bert to be made into an archer's quiver.
explanation.walkthrough: Quiver looks like a noun, the arrow case a chopped elm might become; it is the verb meaning to shake.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: both mean to shake slightly, as with fear or cold, not the archer's arrow case.

blocks.note: frank = forthright
to incense is to anger

explanation.surface: Being handed a second present provokes a blunt, angry response.
explanation.walkthrough: Second gift points to the Nativity story: the three wise men brought gold, frankincense and myrrh, in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: in the Gospel of Matthew the Magi's gifts are listed as gold, then this aromatic resin, then myrrh.

indicators.note: the king's letter goes inside the figure

blocks.note: a statue is a sculpted figure
R = rex, king; it goes in before the last letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to construct a statue of a monarch indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Build looks like a verb telling you to put up a statue; it is the noun for someone's size and frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym in the noun sense: a person's build and their height and bodily frame overlap.

clue.text: Flowers untidily spilt around top of urn (6)

indicators.note: the letters of spilt are put back untidily
the jumbled letters go around the U
the top of a down-standing word is its first letter

blocks.note: SPILT rearranged
first letter of urn, placed after the first letter of the jumble

explanation.surface: Flowers have tumbled out of a vase and lie scattered around its rim.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a knocked-over vase of flowers; the urn only gives its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: these cup-shaped spring blooms are one kind of flower.

clue.text: Break for refreshment at mine's entrance (3,4)

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine, plus the possessive S
the entrance to a mine shaft is at its top

explanation.surface: Miners pause for a snack at the pithead.
explanation.walkthrough: The mine's entrance is the pit's top, and the same letters respaced give the answer. The definition uses the informal sense of a quick stop on a journey rather than a racing car's.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal extension: the motor-racing term for a quick halt is borrowed for a short break in a journey to eat or drink.

blocks.note: a slang verb: to catch sight of
the ordinary noun for instruments that tell the time

explanation.walkthrough: Notices looks like a plural noun, signs on a wall; it is the verb, as in 'she clocks the newcomer at once'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: British slang uses clock to mean notice or spot, and the plain noun names timepieces.

clue.text: One provides for pet before two queens (7)

definitions.note: the definition is a clause describing the person

blocks.note: a cat is a pet
ER = Elizabeth Regina, twice

explanation.surface: Someone feeds a pet before attending to two queens.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'provides for pet' as feeding an animal, but the definition stops at 'for': one who provides for others, especially food at events.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: to cater for people is to provide for them, and the answer is the person who does it.

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word run into the first four of the second

explanation.surface: A lament that some old-fashioned stiffening agent has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Archaic and lost both suggest something forgotten, which makes the phrase look like a description rather than a string of letters to look inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A description by function: this powder is used in laundry to stiffen collars and linen.

clue.text: Like perfect vision of modern cricket? (6-6)

blocks.note: the eye-test score for normal, sharp sight
the short, modern form of cricket, twenty overs a side

explanation.surface: A question whether today's cricket is seen perfectly clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: Twenty20 is cricket's newest professional format, with each side batting for just twenty overs, and 20/20 is the eye test's score for normal sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: 20/20 vision is the standard for sharp eyesight, and Twenty20 is the short format of cricket.

indicators.note: the answer is inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A remark about how words are ordered in Chinese dictionaries.
explanation.walkthrough: Order reads as the arrangement of entries in a dictionary; it is a decree.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of a command: this is an official decree issued by an authority.

clue.text: Hear Roman forty do really well (5)

indicators.note: the letters are what you hear, not what you see

blocks.note: XL is forty in Roman numerals; said as letters, 'ex-ell'

explanation.surface: A teacher's encouragement: listen, Roman numeral forty, and you'll do well.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the Roman numeral letter by letter and you get the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to surpass others or be outstanding at something.

indicators.note: the answer is inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word run into the first two of the second

explanation.surface: A decorative antique painted in colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Fancy sits there like an anagram indicator, but no rearranging is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this greenish blue, one of the printer's inks, is one colour among many.

indicators.note: the one goes into the rota

blocks.note: a roster is a rota
I = one, placed after the second letter

explanation.surface: Someone struts about once their name is put on the duty rota.
explanation.walkthrough: Rota is not itself the letters; swap it for its synonym before the one goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the old verb means to revel noisily and boisterously, which shades into swaggering.

blocks.note: coy = bashful
RN = Royal Navy, placed before the last letter

explanation.surface: A shy sailor is embarrassed at being called clichéd.
explanation.walkthrough: Navy sounds like a colour or a fleet; here it is the abbreviation for the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something trite and overused, like a stale joke.

blocks.note: the surface wants a topic for debate; the setter means offspring, as in 'died without issue'
not legal adoption but taking on a partner's children by marriage

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline about the topic of adoption.
explanation.walkthrough: Issue reads as a topic for debate; in family law it means children, and the ones you take on, or adopt, by marrying their parent are stepchildren.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose, playful fit: children acquired through marrying their parent are in a sense adopted, and issue means offspring.
